Unit 2 · 12–17% of exam

Economic Indicators and the Business Cycle

2.1

2.1 The Circular Flow and GDP

  • The circular flow model links households and firms through two markets. In the product market, households buy goods and services from firms. In the factor market, firms pay households wages, rent, interest, and profit for labor, land, capital, and entrepreneurship.
  • Government, the financial sector, and the foreign sector add leakages (taxes, saving, imports) and injections (government purchases, investment, exports).
  • GDP is the market value of all final goods and services produced within a country's borders in a given period, usually one year.
  • Three approaches give the same total: expenditures (), income (wages + rent + interest + profit), and value added (the sum of the value added at each stage of production).
  • Investment () is business spending on capital goods, new construction (including new homes), and changes in inventories. Government purchases () exclude transfer payments.
  • Not counted: intermediate goods, used goods, purely financial transactions such as stocks and bonds, transfer payments, unpaid household work, and illegal or unreported activity.
Expenditures approach

Watch outBuying shares of stock is not investment in the GDP sense. Imports are subtracted because they were already counted inside , , or but were not produced domestically.

Practice 2.1 · 2 questions

2.2

2.2 Limitations of GDP

  • GDP measures output, not well-being. It leaves out nonmarket activity (household production, volunteer work), the underground economy, leisure time, and environmental damage.
  • GDP says nothing about how income is distributed or what kinds of goods are produced.
  • GDP can rise because of bad events, such as cleanup spending after a disaster.
  • GDP per capita (GDP divided by population) is a better, though still imperfect, indicator of the standard of living than total GDP.

Watch outWhen paid work is replaced by unpaid work (or the reverse), measured GDP changes even though the amount of production does not.

Practice 2.2 · 2 questions

2.3

2.3 Unemployment

  • The labor force is everyone 16 or older who is employed or unemployed. To count as unemployed, a person must have no job, be available for work, and have actively looked for work in the past four weeks.
  • People not in the labor force include full-time students, retirees, stay-at-home parents, and discouraged workers who have stopped looking.
  • Frictional unemployment: people between jobs or entering the labor force. Structural: skills or locations do not match available jobs, often because of technology or shifts in demand. Cyclical: caused by a recession.
  • The natural rate of unemployment is frictional plus structural unemployment. It is the unemployment rate when the economy produces full-employment output, so cyclical unemployment is zero. It can change slowly over time.
  • The official rate can understate joblessness because it ignores discouraged workers and counts part-time workers who want full-time work as employed.
Labor force
Unemployment rate
Participation rate

Watch outDivide the number of unemployed by the labor force, never by the whole population. Full employment does not mean zero unemployment.

Practice 2.3 · 3 questions

2.4

2.4 Price Indices and Inflation

  • The consumer price index (CPI) compares the cost of a fixed market basket of goods and services with its cost in a base year. The base-year CPI is 100.
  • Inflation is a sustained rise in the overall price level. Deflation is a falling price level. Disinflation is a falling inflation rate while prices still rise.
  • Real values are adjusted for price changes; nominal values are not. Percent change in real income is about the percent change in nominal income minus the inflation rate.
  • The CPI tends to overstate inflation because of substitution bias (the basket is fixed even when consumers switch to cheaper goods), new products, and unmeasured quality improvements.
CPI
Inflation rate
Deflating

Watch outThe inflation rate is a percent change, not the change in index points. Always divide by the earlier CPI.

Practice 2.4 · 4 questions

2.5

2.5 Costs of Inflation

  • Unexpected inflation arbitrarily redistributes wealth. Borrowers with fixed-rate loans gain because they repay with dollars that buy less. Lenders, savers earning fixed interest, people on fixed incomes, and holders of cash lose.
  • Unexpected deflation or disinflation does the reverse: lenders gain and borrowers lose.
  • If inflation is correctly anticipated, lenders build it into nominal interest rates and workers into wage contracts, so little wealth is redistributed.
  • Inflation also erodes the purchasing power of money and creates uncertainty that discourages long-term contracts and investment.
Real interest rate

Practice 2.5 · 2 questions

2.6

2.6 Real v. Nominal GDP

  • Nominal GDP values this year's output at this year's prices. It can rise because of more output, higher prices, or both.
  • Real GDP values this year's output at base-year prices, so it changes only when output changes. Economic growth is measured with real GDP.
  • The GDP deflator is a price index for all goods and services in GDP. In the base year, nominal GDP equals real GDP and the deflator is 100.
  • Percent change in nominal GDP is about the percent change in real GDP plus the inflation rate.
Nominal GDP
Real GDP
GDP deflator

Practice 2.6 · 3 questions

2.7

2.7 Business Cycles

  • The business cycle is the fluctuation of real GDP around its long-run growth trend. Phases: expansion and recession (contraction). Turning points: peak and trough.
  • Potential output, also called full-employment output, is real GDP when unemployment equals the natural rate.
  • The output gap is actual output minus potential output. A negative (recessionary) gap means output is below potential and unemployment is above the natural rate. A positive (inflationary) gap means output is above potential and unemployment is below the natural rate.
  • In a recession, real GDP falls and cyclical unemployment rises. Near a peak, unemployment is low and inflation pressure is high.
Output gap

Unit 3 · 17–27% of exam

National Income and Price Determination

3.1

3.1 Aggregate Demand (AD)

  • Aggregate demand shows the total real GDP demanded by households, firms, government, and the rest of the world at each price level.
  • AD slopes downward for three reasons. Real wealth effect: a lower price level raises the purchasing power of money and assets, so consumption rises. Interest rate effect: a lower price level lowers interest rates, so investment rises. Exchange rate effect: a lower price level makes domestic goods cheaper relative to foreign goods, so net exports rise.
  • A change in the price level causes a movement along AD. A change in , , , or at every price level shifts AD.
  • AD shifts right when consumer or business confidence rises, wealth rises, taxes fall, government purchases rise, interest rates fall for reasons other than the price level, trading partners' incomes rise, or the domestic currency depreciates.

Watch outA change in the price level never shifts AD. It only moves the economy along the curve.

Practice 3.1 · 2 questions

3.2

3.2 Multipliers

  • The marginal propensity to consume (MPC) is the fraction of each extra dollar of disposable income that is spent. The marginal propensity to save (MPS) is the fraction saved.
  • An initial change in spending sets off rounds of further spending, so GDP changes by a multiple of the initial change. The expenditure multiplier applies to autonomous changes in , , , or .
  • The tax multiplier is smaller in size because households save part of any tax cut before spending the rest. Its sign is negative: taxes and GDP move in opposite directions. Transfer payments use the same size multiplier with a positive sign.
  • Equal increases in government purchases and taxes raise GDP by the amount of the increase (balanced-budget multiplier of 1).
  • A larger MPC means larger multipliers.
MPC and MPS
Expenditure multiplier
Tax multiplier
Total effect

ExampleWith MPC = 0.9, the expenditure multiplier is and the tax multiplier is . A $10 billion rise in government purchases raises GDP by up to $100 billion; a $10 billion tax cut raises it by up to $90 billion.

Practice 3.2 · 3 questions

3.3

3.3 Short-Run Aggregate Supply (SRAS)

  • Short-run aggregate supply shows the total real GDP firms produce at each price level while some input prices are fixed.
  • SRAS slopes upward because nominal wages and other input prices are sticky in the short run. When the price level rises and costs do not, profit per unit rises and firms produce more.
  • Moving along SRAS involves a short-run trade-off: higher output and lower unemployment come with a higher price level.
  • SRAS shifts when production costs change at every price level: input prices (wages, oil, raw materials), productivity, business taxes, subsidies, regulation, and expected inflation. Higher costs shift SRAS left; lower costs shift it right.

Watch outA change in the price level is a movement along SRAS, not a shift.

Practice 3.3 · 2 questions

3.4

3.4 Long-Run Aggregate Supply (LRAS)

  • In the long run all wages and prices are fully flexible, so output returns to full-employment (potential) output whatever the price level. The LRAS curve is vertical at potential output.
  • LRAS matches the production possibilities curve: it shifts right when the economy's productive capacity grows.
  • LRAS shifts with the quantity and quality of resources (labor, physical capital, natural resources), human capital, and technology. A rightward shift is economic growth.
  • Changes in the price level or in aggregate demand do not shift LRAS.

Watch outAnything that raises potential output, such as better technology, shifts both LRAS and SRAS to the right.

Practice 3.4 · 2 questions

3.5

3.5 Equilibrium in the AD–AS Model

  • Short-run equilibrium is where AD crosses SRAS. It sets the price level and real GDP.
  • Long-run equilibrium is where AD, SRAS, and LRAS all cross. Output equals potential and unemployment equals the natural rate.
  • Recessionary (negative output) gap: short-run equilibrium output is below potential, to the left of LRAS. Unemployment is above the natural rate.
  • Inflationary (positive output) gap: short-run equilibrium output is above potential, to the right of LRAS. Unemployment is below the natural rate.

Watch outOn a graph, label the vertical axis "price level" and the horizontal axis "real GDP". Full-employment output is where LRAS meets the horizontal axis.

Practice 3.5 · 2 questions

3.6

3.6 Changes in the AD–AS Model in the Short Run

  • AD shifts right (positive demand shock): price level rises, real GDP rises, unemployment falls. Inflation from this source is demand-pull inflation.
  • AD shifts left (negative demand shock): price level falls, real GDP falls, unemployment rises.
  • SRAS shifts left (negative supply shock): price level rises, real GDP falls, unemployment rises. This is cost-push inflation, also called stagflation.
  • SRAS shifts right (positive supply shock): price level falls, real GDP rises, unemployment falls.

Watch outA demand shock moves the price level and output in the same direction. A supply shock moves them in opposite directions.

Practice 3.6 · 3 questions

3.7

3.7 Long-Run Self-Adjustment

  • With no policy action, flexible wages and prices move the economy back to potential output. The adjustment happens through shifts of SRAS.
  • Recessionary gap: high unemployment pushes nominal wages down over time. Lower costs shift SRAS right until output returns to potential at a lower price level.
  • Inflationary gap: a tight labor market pushes nominal wages up. Higher costs shift SRAS left until output returns to potential at a higher price level.
  • In the long run a shift in AD changes only the price level. Real GDP returns to potential and unemployment returns to the natural rate.
  • A shift of LRAS changes potential output itself and represents long-run growth or decline.

Watch outSelf-adjustment works through wages and SRAS. AD does not shift by itself to close a gap.

Practice 3.7 · 2 questions

3.8

3.8 Fiscal Policy

  • Fiscal policy is the use of government purchases, taxes, and transfer payments to influence aggregate demand.
  • Expansionary policy fights a recessionary gap: raise government purchases, cut taxes, or raise transfers. AD shifts right, so real GDP and the price level rise and unemployment falls. The budget moves toward deficit.
  • Contractionary policy fights an inflationary gap: cut government purchases, raise taxes, or cut transfers. AD shifts left, so real GDP and the price level fall. The budget moves toward surplus.
  • Government purchases affect AD directly. Taxes and transfers work indirectly through disposable income and consumption, so a dollar of spending has a larger effect than a dollar of tax change.
  • Discretionary policy has lags: time to recognize the problem, to pass legislation, and for the change to take effect.
Sizing a spending change
Sizing a tax change

Practice 3.8 · 4 questions

3.9

3.9 Automatic Stabilizers

  • Automatic stabilizers are taxes and transfer programs that change with the business cycle without any new legislation.
  • In a recession, incomes fall, so income tax revenue falls and spending on programs such as unemployment insurance rises. Disposable income and consumption fall by less, which cushions the drop in AD. The deficit grows automatically.
  • In an expansion, tax revenue rises and transfer payments fall, which restrains AD and keeps the economy from overheating.
  • Stabilizers reduce the size of business-cycle swings but do not eliminate them. Unlike discretionary policy, they have no decision lag.

Watch outA stimulus bill passed by Congress is discretionary policy, not an automatic stabilizer.

Practice 3.9 · 2 questions

Unit 1 · 7–9% of exam

Atomic Structure and Properties

1.1

1.1 Moles and Molar Mass

  • The mole connects the mass of a sample to the number of particles in it. One mole contains particles, which is Avogadro's number ().
  • Molar mass in g/mol has the same numerical value as the average mass of one atom or molecule in amu.
  • Use dimensional analysis to move between grams, moles, and particles. Use the subscripts in a formula to go from molecules to atoms.
Moles from mass
Particles from moles

Watch outCheck whether a question asks for atoms or molecules. One mole of contains two moles of oxygen atoms.

Practice 1.1 · 2 questions

1.2

1.2 Mass Spectra of Elements

  • The mass spectrum of an element has one peak for each isotope. A peak's position gives the isotope's mass, and its height gives the isotope's relative abundance.
  • Isotopes of an element have the same number of protons and different numbers of neutrons.
  • Average atomic mass is the abundance-weighted average of the isotope masses. It lies closest to the mass of the most abundant isotope.
Weighted average

Watch outDo not take a simple average of the isotope masses. Convert each percent to a decimal and weight each mass.

Practice 1.2 · 2 questions

1.3

1.3 Elemental Composition of Pure Substances

  • A pure substance has a fixed composition. The law of definite proportions says a compound always contains the same elements in the same ratio by mass.
  • The empirical formula is the lowest whole-number ratio of atoms. The molecular formula is a whole-number multiple of it.
  • To find an empirical formula: treat percents as grams in a 100 g sample, convert to moles, divide by the smallest number of moles, and scale to whole numbers.
Mass percent
Molecular formula

Watch outConvert masses to moles before taking ratios. A ratio of grams is not a ratio of atoms.

Practice 1.3 · 2 questions

1.4

1.4 Composition of Mixtures

  • A mixture contains two or more substances whose proportions can vary. A pure substance has one fixed composition.
  • Elemental analysis measures the mass percent of each element in a sample. Comparing the result with the percent calculated for the pure compound shows whether the sample is pure.
  • If the measured percent of an element is too low, the impurity contains a smaller percent of that element than the compound does (or none). If it is too high, the impurity contains a larger percent.
Mixture composition

Practice 1.4 · 2 questions

1.5

1.5 Atomic Structure and Electron Configuration

  • An atom has a dense nucleus of protons and neutrons surrounded by electrons. Electrons are held by the attraction between opposite charges.
  • Coulomb's law: the force between two charges grows with the size of the charges and shrinks as the distance between them grows.
  • Electrons fill subshells from lowest energy up (Aufbau principle): , , , , , , , . An subshell holds 2 electrons, holds 6, and holds 10.
  • Core electrons are in inner shells. Valence electrons are in the outermost occupied shell.
  • To write a cation's configuration, remove electrons from the highest shell first. Transition metals lose their electrons before their electrons.
  • Ionization energy is the energy needed to remove an electron from an atom or ion in the gas phase.
Coulomb's law

Watch out is . The two electrons are removed, not two electrons.

Practice 1.5 · 3 questions

1.6

1.6 Photoelectron Spectroscopy

  • Photoelectron spectroscopy (PES) measures the energy needed to remove electrons from each subshell of an atom.
  • Each peak is one subshell. The peak's position is the binding energy: electrons closer to the nucleus have higher binding energy, so is always highest.
  • The peak's height is proportional to the number of electrons in that subshell.
  • Reading the peak heights in order gives the electron configuration and identifies the element.
  • For the same subshell, an atom with more protons has a higher binding energy.

Watch outHeight tells you how many electrons. Position tells you how strongly they are held. Check which direction the energy axis runs before reading a spectrum.

Practice 1.6 · 2 questions

1.7

1.7 Periodic Trends

  • Trends follow from Coulomb's law: the attraction depends on effective nuclear charge and on the distance of the valence electrons from the nucleus (the number of shells).
  • Atomic radius decreases across a period (more protons pulling on the same shell) and increases down a group (more shells).
  • First ionization energy increases across a period and decreases down a group. Electronegativity follows the same pattern; fluorine is highest.
  • Ionic radius: cations are smaller than their atoms and anions are larger. In an isoelectronic series, the ion with the most protons is the smallest.
  • Successive ionization energies rise steadily, then jump sharply when the first core electron is removed. The number of electrons removed before the jump is the number of valence electrons.
  • Electron affinity generally becomes more negative across a period.

Watch outExplain a trend with protons, shells, and attraction. Saying an atom "wants a full octet" or naming the trend is not an explanation.

Practice 1.7 · 4 questions

1.8

1.8 Valence Electrons and Ionic Compounds

  • Elements in the same group have the same number of valence electrons, so they react in similar ways and form compounds with similar formulas, such as and .
  • Typical ion charges: group 1 forms 1+, group 2 forms 2+, group 13 forms 3+, group 15 forms 3−, group 16 forms 2−, group 17 forms 1−.
  • The formula of an ionic compound is the smallest whole-number ratio of ions that gives a total charge of zero.

Example and need a total of 6+ and 6−, so the formula is .

Practice 1.8 · 2 questions

Unit 2 · 7–9% of exam

Compound Structure and Properties

2.1

2.1 Types of Chemical Bonds

  • Electronegativity is an atom's ability to attract shared electrons. The difference in electronegativity between two bonded atoms sets the bond type.
  • Nonpolar covalent: electrons shared equally (identical atoms or very similar electronegativity). Polar covalent: electrons shared unequally, giving partial charges. Ionic: electrons transferred, usually between a metal and a nonmetal. Metallic: valence electrons delocalized among metal atoms.
  • The greater the electronegativity difference, the more polar the bond. The more electronegative atom carries the partial negative charge.
  • Bonding is a continuum. The properties of a substance, such as conductivity when melted, are the best evidence for its bond type.

Practice 2.1 · 3 questions

2.2

2.2 Intramolecular Force and Potential Energy

  • A graph of potential energy versus the distance between two nuclei has a minimum. The distance at the minimum is the bond length, and the depth of the minimum is the bond energy, the energy needed to break the bond.
  • At shorter distances, repulsion raises the potential energy sharply. At large distances the atoms do not interact and the potential energy approaches zero.
  • Higher bond order means a shorter and stronger bond: triple < double < single in length.
  • For ions, Coulomb's law applies: attraction is stronger when the charges are larger and the ions are smaller (closer together).

Watch outA stronger bond sits lower on the potential energy graph (a deeper well), not higher.

Practice 2.2 · 3 questions

2.3

2.3 Structure of Ionic Solids

  • An ionic solid is a three-dimensional lattice of alternating cations and anions. The arrangement maximizes attraction between opposite charges and minimizes repulsion between like charges.
  • Ionic solids have high melting points and are hard but brittle.
  • They do not conduct electricity as solids because the ions are fixed in place. They conduct when melted or dissolved because the ions can move.
  • There are no separate molecules. The formula gives the ratio of ions.

Practice 2.3 · 2 questions

2.4

2.4 Structure of Metals and Alloys

  • In a metal, positive metal ions sit in a lattice surrounded by a sea of delocalized valence electrons.
  • Mobile electrons explain electrical and thermal conductivity. Because the bonding is not directional, layers can slide without breaking the solid, so metals are malleable and ductile.
  • Interstitial alloy: small atoms fill the spaces between larger metal atoms, as carbon does in steel. The result is usually harder and less malleable.
  • Substitutional alloy: atoms of similar size replace some of the metal atoms, as zinc does in brass.

Watch outUse atomic radius to decide the alloy type: much smaller atoms give an interstitial alloy; similar-sized atoms give a substitutional alloy.

Practice 2.4 · 2 questions

2.5

2.5 Lewis Diagrams

  • Count the total valence electrons, adding one for each negative charge and subtracting one for each positive charge.
  • Join the atoms with single bonds (least electronegative atom in the center, never hydrogen), complete the octets of the outer atoms, and place any remaining electrons on the central atom.
  • If the central atom lacks an octet, turn lone pairs on outer atoms into double or triple bonds.
  • Exceptions to the octet rule: hydrogen holds 2 electrons; boron and beryllium may have fewer than 8; elements in period 3 and below may hold more than 8.

Practice 2.5 · 2 questions

2.6

2.6 Resonance and Formal Charge

  • Resonance occurs when two or more valid Lewis diagrams differ only in where the electrons are placed. The real molecule is an average of them, called a resonance hybrid.
  • In a resonance hybrid the electrons are delocalized, and the bonds involved are identical, with lengths and strengths between those of single and double bonds.
  • Formal charge helps choose the best diagram. Prefer formal charges closest to zero, with any negative formal charge on the more electronegative atom. Formal charges add up to the overall charge.
Formal charge

Watch outA molecule does not flip back and forth between resonance structures. It has one structure, the hybrid.

Practice 2.6 · 2 questions

2.7

2.7 VSEPR and Hybridization

  • VSEPR: electron domains around a central atom spread as far apart as possible. A domain is a lone pair or a bond; a double or triple bond counts as one domain.
  • 2 domains: linear, 180°, . 3 domains: trigonal planar, 120°, ; with one lone pair the shape is bent. 4 domains: tetrahedral, 109.5°, ; one lone pair gives trigonal pyramidal (about 107°); two give bent (about 104.5°).
  • 5 domains: trigonal bipyramidal (90° and 120°); lone pairs give seesaw, T-shaped, then linear. 6 domains: octahedral (90°); lone pairs give square pyramidal, then square planar.
  • Lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs, so they squeeze the bond angles.
  • A single bond is one sigma (σ) bond. A double bond is one σ and one pi (π) bond. A triple bond is one σ and two π bonds.
  • A molecule is polar when its bond dipoles do not cancel. Symmetric shapes with identical outer atoms, such as , , and , are nonpolar.

Watch outCount domains on the central atom from the Lewis diagram first. Name the molecular shape from the positions of the atoms only, not the lone pairs.

Practice 2.7 · 5 questions

Unit 3 · 18–22% of exam

Properties of Substances and Mixtures

3.1

3.1 Intermolecular and Interparticle Forces

  • London dispersion forces act between all particles. They come from temporary dipoles and grow stronger with more electrons (a more polarizable electron cloud) and with more surface contact between molecules.
  • Dipole–dipole forces act between polar molecules.
  • Hydrogen bonding is a strong dipole–dipole attraction: a hydrogen atom bonded to N, O, or F is attracted to a lone pair on N, O, or F in another molecule.
  • Ion–dipole forces act between ions and polar molecules, as when a salt dissolves in water.
  • Stronger intermolecular forces mean a higher boiling point, higher melting point, and lower vapor pressure.

Watch outBoiling a molecular substance separates molecules from each other. It does not break the covalent bonds inside the molecules.

Practice 3.1 · 3 questions

3.2

3.2 Properties of Solids

  • Ionic solids: ions held by strong electrostatic attraction. High melting point, brittle, conduct only when melted or dissolved.
  • Molecular solids: separate molecules held by intermolecular forces. Low melting point, soft, do not conduct. Examples: ice, , dry ice, sugar.
  • Covalent network solids: atoms joined by covalent bonds throughout the whole solid. Very high melting point and very hard. Examples: diamond, , .
  • Metallic solids: metal ions in a sea of electrons. Conduct as solids and are malleable.
  • Graphite is a network solid made of sheets. Each carbon bonds to three others, and the leftover electrons are delocalized, so graphite conducts and its sheets slide.
  • Crystalline solids have an ordered, repeating arrangement. Amorphous solids do not.

Practice 3.2 · 3 questions

3.3

3.3 Solids, Liquids, and Gases

  • Solid: particles packed closely in fixed positions; they only vibrate. Fixed shape and volume.
  • Liquid: particles close together but able to move past one another. Fixed volume, takes the shape of its container.
  • Gas: particles far apart, moving constantly and randomly, with negligible attractions. Fills its container and is easily compressed.
  • The solid and liquid phases of a substance have similar molar volumes because the particles are in close contact in both.
  • The phase depends on the balance between intermolecular forces and the kinetic energy of the particles.

Practice 3.3 · 2 questions

3.4

3.4 Ideal Gas Law

  • The ideal gas law relates pressure, volume, moles, and temperature. Temperature must be in kelvin.
  • With moles fixed, use the combined gas law. Pressure and volume are inversely related; volume and pressure are each directly related to kelvin temperature.
  • Dalton's law: the total pressure of a gas mixture is the sum of the partial pressures. Each partial pressure equals the gas's mole fraction times the total pressure.
  • At STP (273 K and 1 atm), one mole of an ideal gas occupies about 22.4 L.
Ideal gas law
Combined gas law
Dalton's law
Molar mass from density

Watch outConvert Celsius to kelvin before using any gas law: .

Practice 3.4 · 4 questions

3.5

3.5 Kinetic Molecular Theory

  • Gas particles are in constant, random motion. An ideal gas has particles of negligible volume, with no attractions between them and perfectly elastic collisions.
  • Pressure comes from collisions of particles with the container walls.
  • The average kinetic energy of gas particles depends only on the kelvin temperature. All gases at the same temperature have the same average kinetic energy.
  • At the same temperature, lighter particles move faster on average.
  • A Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution shows the spread of particle speeds. Raising the temperature makes the curve broader and flatter and moves its peak to higher speed.
Kinetic energy

Practice 3.5 · 2 questions

3.6

3.6 Deviation from Ideal Gas Law

  • Real gases deviate from ideal behavior most at low temperature and high pressure, when particles are slow and close together.
  • Attractive forces between particles make the measured pressure lower than the ideal prediction, because particles strike the walls with less force.
  • Particle volume matters at very high pressure. The particles take up part of the container, so the measured pressure is higher than the ideal prediction.
  • Gases behave most ideally at high temperature and low pressure. Small particles with weak attractions, such as He, come closest to ideal.

Practice 3.6 · 2 questions

3.7

3.7 Solutions and Mixtures

  • A solution is a homogeneous mixture: its composition is uniform throughout at the particle level. A heterogeneous mixture has regions with different compositions.
  • Solutions can be solids (alloys), liquids, or gases (air).
  • Molarity is moles of solute per liter of solution.
  • Diluting a solution adds solvent but leaves the moles of solute unchanged.
Molarity
Dilution

Watch outMolarity uses liters of solution, not liters of solvent. Convert mL to L.

Practice 3.7 · 2 questions

3.8

3.8 Representations of Solutions

  • A particulate drawing of a solution should show the correct relative numbers of solute particles and how the solute and solvent particles interact.
  • Soluble ionic compounds separate into individual ions in water, in the ratio given by the formula. Molecular solutes such as sugar stay as whole molecules.
  • Water molecules orient around ions: the oxygen end (partial negative) points toward cations, and the hydrogen ends (partial positive) point toward anions. These are ion–dipole attractions.

Watch outDo not draw dissolved ionic compounds as molecules. (aq) is one ion and two separate ions, not .

Practice 3.8 · 2 questions

3.9

3.9 Separation of Solutions and Mixtures

  • Separation methods use differences in intermolecular forces and physical properties.
  • Filtration separates an undissolved solid from a liquid. It cannot remove a dissolved solute.
  • Evaporation recovers a dissolved solid by removing the solvent.
  • Distillation separates liquids with different boiling points. The component with weaker intermolecular forces vaporizes first.
  • Chromatography separates components that are attracted differently to a mobile phase (the moving solvent) and a stationary phase (such as paper). A component attracted more to the mobile phase travels farther.

Practice 3.9 · 2 questions

3.10

3.10 Solubility

  • Substances with similar intermolecular forces tend to dissolve in each other: "like dissolves like."
  • Ionic and polar solutes dissolve in polar solvents such as water. Nonpolar solutes dissolve in nonpolar solvents such as hexane.
  • A solute dissolves when solute–solvent attractions are about as strong as the solute–solute and solvent–solvent attractions they replace.
  • Molecules that can hydrogen-bond with water, such as small alcohols, are very soluble. A longer nonpolar carbon chain lowers solubility in water.

Practice 3.10 · 2 questions

3.11

3.11 Spectroscopy and the Electromagnetic Spectrum

  • Different regions of the electromagnetic spectrum cause different changes in molecules and atoms.
  • Microwave radiation changes how molecules rotate.
  • Infrared radiation changes how bonds vibrate. It is used to identify the types of bonds in a molecule.
  • Ultraviolet and visible radiation move electrons between energy levels.
  • From lowest to highest photon energy: microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet.

Practice 3.11 · 2 questions

3.12

3.12 Properties of Photons

  • Light has wave properties: wavelength () and frequency () are inversely related through the speed of light.
  • Light also comes in packets of energy called photons. Higher frequency, or shorter wavelength, means more energy per photon.
  • An atom or molecule absorbs or emits a photon only when the photon's energy equals the difference between two of its energy levels.
Wave equation
Photon energy

Watch outConvert nanometers to meters before calculating: .

Practice 3.12 · 3 questions

3.13

3.13 Beer–Lambert Law

  • Absorbance is proportional to concentration. is the molar absorptivity (how strongly the substance absorbs at that wavelength), is the path length, and is the concentration.
  • With the same substance, cuvette, and wavelength, absorbance and concentration are directly proportional. A graph of absorbance versus concentration for known solutions (a calibration curve) is a straight line used to find an unknown concentration.
  • Measure at the wavelength where the substance absorbs most strongly.
  • Common errors: a smudged cuvette scatters light and raises the absorbance reading; water left in the cuvette dilutes the sample and lowers it.
Beer–Lambert law

Question 21. In paper chromatography, a mixture of dyes is separated using a nonpolar solvent as the mobile phase and polar paper as the stationary phase. The dye that travels farthest up the paper is the one that is

Explanation
A less polar dye interacts weakly with the polar paper and dissolves well in the nonpolar solvent, so it moves with the solvent.

Explanation

Mixing iodine with water would mean breaking strong hydrogen bonds between water molecules and replacing them with weaker attractions. Hexane and iodine interact through similar dispersion forces.

AP United States History · Periods 1–2

US History notes

NotesPractice · 44 questions

Period 1 · 4–6% of exam

1491–1607

1.1

1.1 Contextualizing Period 1

  • In 1491 the Americas were home to millions of people living in diverse, complex societies shaped by their environments. They had no contact with Europe or Africa.
  • Changes in Europe set up exploration: stronger centralized monarchies (Spain completed its unification in 1492), demand for Asian trade goods and a sea route to reach them, the Renaissance and new maritime technology, and religious rivalry sharpened by the Protestant Reformation (1517).
  • Portugal's voyages along the West African coast opened new trade, including a trade in enslaved people.
  • Columbus's voyage in 1492 began lasting contact among Europeans, Native Americans, and Africans. The period ends in 1607 with Jamestown, the first permanent English settlement.

Watch outContextualization means describing the broader setting of a development: what was already happening, and why it matters for what came next.

Practice 1.1 · 2 questions

1.2

1.2 Native American Societies Before European Contact

  • Native peoples adapted to and transformed their environments, which produced very different societies in different regions.
  • Maize cultivation spread north from present-day Mexico. In the Southwest it supported settled communities, irrigation, and social diversification (Pueblo peoples).
  • In the Great Basin and on the western Great Plains, dry land and scarce resources led to largely mobile lifestyles based on hunting and gathering.
  • In the Northeast, the Mississippi River Valley, and along the Atlantic seaboard, societies mixed farming with hunting and gathering and built permanent villages. Examples: the Iroquois (Haudenosaunee) and the Mississippian city of Cahokia.
  • In the Northwest and present-day California, peoples lived by hunting, gathering, and fishing; rich ocean resources supported settled communities such as those of the Chinook.

Watch outTie each region to its environment. The exam asks how geography shaped a society's economy and settlement pattern.

Practice 1.2 · 3 questions

1.3

1.3 European Exploration in the Americas

  • European states explored for wealth, power, and religion: new sources of gold and trade, an edge over rival kingdoms, and converts to Christianity.
  • Portugal led early, sailing around Africa to reach Asia. Spain backed Columbus's westward voyage in 1492.
  • The Treaty of Tordesillas (1494) divided newly claimed lands between Spain and Portugal.
  • New technology made long voyages possible: the caravel, the compass, the astrolabe, and better maps.
  • France and England began exploring later, looking for a northwest passage to Asia.

Practice 1.3 · 2 questions

1.4

1.4 Columbian Exchange, Spanish Exploration, and Conquest

  • The Columbian Exchange was the transfer of plants, animals, people, and diseases between the Eastern and Western Hemispheres after 1492.
  • To the Americas: horses, cattle, pigs, wheat, sugar cane, and diseases such as smallpox and measles. Epidemics killed a large share of the Native population.
  • To Europe, Africa, and Asia: maize, potatoes, tomatoes, cacao, and tobacco. The new food crops supported population growth.
  • Gold and silver from the Americas and expanded trade helped Europe shift from feudalism toward capitalism.
  • Spanish conquistadors toppled the Aztec Empire (Cortés, 1519–1521) and the Inca Empire (Pizarro, 1530s), helped by disease, steel weapons, horses, and Native allies.

Practice 1.4 · 3 questions

1.5

1.5 Labor, Slavery, and Caste in the Spanish Colonial System

  • Under the encomienda system, the Spanish crown granted colonists the right to demand labor and tribute from Native Americans in a given area, in return for supposedly protecting and Christianizing them. In practice it meant forced labor in fields and mines.
  • As disease and overwork reduced the Native population, and as the crown tried to limit abuses (the New Laws of 1542), the Spanish turned increasingly to enslaved Africans for plantation and mining labor.
  • The Spanish developed a casta system that ranked people by racial ancestry: Europeans born in Spain at the top, then American-born Spaniards, then people of mixed ancestry such as mestizos (Spanish and Native American), with Native Americans and Africans at the bottom.

Practice 1.5 · 3 questions

1.6

1.6 Cultural Interactions Between Europeans, Native Americans, and Africans

  • Europeans and Native Americans held different views on religion, gender roles, family, land use, and power. Europeans treated land as private property; many Native societies treated it as a shared resource.
  • Contact brought misunderstanding and conflict, and also exchange: each side adopted useful goods and knowledge from the other.
  • Native peoples defended their sovereignty, economies, and beliefs through both diplomacy and military resistance.
  • Spaniards debated how Native Americans should be treated. Bartolomé de las Casas condemned Spanish cruelty and argued that Native Americans were fully human. Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda argued that they were naturally inferior and that conquest was justified. The two argued their cases in the Valladolid debate (1550–1551).
  • Europeans developed belief systems that justified the subjugation of Africans and Native Americans.

Practice 1.6 · 2 questions

1.7

1.7 Causation in Period 1

  • Causes of exploration: competition among European states, the search for wealth and trade routes, religious zeal, and new technology.
  • Effects in the Americas: the Columbian Exchange, epidemic disease and population collapse, Spanish conquest, forced-labor systems, and the growth of the Atlantic slave trade.
  • Effects in Europe: new crops and population growth, new wealth, the growth of capitalism, and sharper rivalry as other states sought their own colonies.

Watch outFor causation questions, separate immediate effects from long-term effects, and be ready to say which cause mattered most and why.

Practice 1.7 · 2 questions

Period 2 · 6–8% of exam

1607–1754

2.1

2.1 Contextualizing Period 2

  • Spain, France, the Netherlands, and England built colonies in North America with different goals, methods, and relations with Native peoples.
  • The British colonies grew quickly through migration and natural increase. They developed distinct regional economies, tied themselves to Atlantic trade, and came to rely on enslaved labor.
  • Colonists built habits of self-government while Britain enforced its rules loosely.
  • The period runs from the founding of Jamestown (1607) to the start of the French and Indian War (1754).

Practice 2.1 · 2 questions

2.2

2.2 European Colonization

  • Spanish: sought wealth and converts. They built missions and forts, subjugated Native peoples, and brought them into colonial society. Settlements included St. Augustine (1565) and Santa Fe (1610).
  • French: few settlers. They relied on the fur trade, alliances, and intermarriage with American Indians. Quebec was founded in 1608.
  • Dutch: few settlers and a commercial focus. New Netherland was a trading colony centered on New Amsterdam; England seized it in 1664 and renamed it New York.
  • English: large numbers of men and women migrated, seeking land, economic opportunity, and religious freedom. They farmed, took land from Native peoples, and lived apart from them.

Practice 2.2 · 4 questions

2.3

2.3 The Regions of British Colonies

  • Chesapeake (Virginia, Maryland) and North Carolina: tobacco, a labor-intensive cash crop. Workers were at first mostly male indentured servants, later enslaved Africans. The House of Burgesses (1619) was the first elected assembly in the English colonies. Maryland was founded as a refuge for Catholics.
  • New England: settled by Puritans who came as families. Small towns, family farms, and a mixed economy of farming, fishing, shipbuilding, and trade. Town meetings gave local self-government. Dissenters such as Roger Williams and Anne Hutchinson were banished; Williams founded Rhode Island.
  • Middle colonies (New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Delaware): exported grain. The most ethnically and religiously diverse region. William Penn founded Pennsylvania as a Quaker colony that practiced religious toleration.
  • Southern Atlantic coast and British West Indies: long growing seasons and plantations growing staple crops such as rice and sugar. Enslaved Africans were often the majority of the population.
  • Distance and loose British oversight let colonies create self-governing institutions that were unusually democratic for the time. In the South, elite planters dominated the assemblies.

Watch outKnow each region's economy, labor system, and settlers. Comparison questions about the regions are common.

Practice 2.3 · 5 questions

2.4

2.4 Transatlantic Trade

  • An Atlantic economy linked Europe, Africa, and the Americas through the exchange of goods, enslaved Africans and American Indians, and ideas. The pattern is often called the triangular trade.
  • Mercantilism held that colonies exist to enrich the home country: they supply raw materials and buy its manufactured goods.
  • The Navigation Acts (beginning in 1651) required trade to be carried on English or colonial ships and required certain colonial goods, such as tobacco and sugar, to be sent only to England.
  • Enforcement was loose and smuggling was common. This period of light British oversight is called salutary neglect.
  • Trade with Europeans brought new goods into American Indian communities and spread epidemic diseases.

Practice 2.4 · 3 questions

2.5

2.5 Interactions Between American Indians and Europeans

  • Relations mixed accommodation and conflict. European powers allied with and armed American Indian groups, who in turn used those alliances against Native rivals.
  • British colonists fought American Indians over land, resources, and boundaries. In Metacom's War (King Philip's War, 1675–1676), the Wampanoag leader Metacom and his allies attacked New England towns; their defeat broke Native power in southern New England.
  • In the Pueblo Revolt (1680), Pueblo peoples drove the Spanish out of New Mexico for more than a decade. After returning, the Spanish accommodated some aspects of Pueblo culture.
  • Trade in furs and guns changed Native economies and intensified warfare among Native groups.

Practice 2.5 · 3 questions

2.6

2.6 Slavery in the British Colonies

  • All British colonies took part in the Atlantic slave trade, driven by abundant land, European demand for colonial goods, and a shortage of indentured servants.
  • New England held relatively few enslaved people. The Chesapeake and the southern Atlantic coast held many. The great majority of enslaved Africans were sent to the West Indies.
  • Bacon's Rebellion (1676) showed Chesapeake planters the danger of a large class of discontented former servants and sped the shift to enslaved African labor.
  • Chattel slavery treated people as property. Laws made slavery hereditary through the mother and created a strict racial system that banned interracial relationships.
  • Enslaved people resisted overtly, as in the Stono Rebellion (South Carolina, 1739), and covertly, by working slowly, breaking tools, running away, and preserving family ties, culture, and religion.

Practice 2.6 · 4 questions

2.7

2.7 Colonial Society and Culture

  • The First Great Awakening (1730s–1740s) was a wave of Protestant revivals led by preachers such as Jonathan Edwards and George Whitefield. It stressed emotional, personal faith, split churches, and encouraged people to question established authority. It was a shared experience across the colonies.
  • The Enlightenment stressed reason and natural rights. John Locke argued that people have natural rights and that government rests on the consent of the governed. Benjamin Franklin embodied Enlightenment thinking in the colonies.
  • Anglicization: the colonies became more like Britain in their political institutions, law, trade, print culture, and Protestant religion.
  • The Zenger trial (1735) was an early victory for freedom of the press.
  • Colonists' resistance to imperial control drew on their experience of self-government, ideas of liberty, the Enlightenment, religious independence, and a belief that the imperial system was corrupt.

Practice 2.7 · 4 questions

2.8

2.8 Comparison in Period 2

  • Chesapeake versus New England: the Chesapeake was settled for profit, mostly by young single men, on scattered tobacco farms, with high death rates and a growing reliance on enslaved labor. New England was settled for religious reasons by families in towns, with a mixed economy and longer lives.
  • Empires: the Spanish converted and subjugated Native peoples; the French and Dutch traded and allied with them; the English came in large numbers and displaced them.
  • Similarities among the British colonies: an English political heritage, elected assemblies, a Protestant majority, participation in Atlantic trade, and conflict with American Indians over land.

Watch outA strong comparison names a specific similarity or difference and explains the reason for it, such as environment, settlers' goals, or the labor system.

Practice 2.8 · 2 questions

Limits and Continuity

1.1

1.1 Introducing Calculus: Can Change Occur at an Instant?

  • The average rate of change of on is the slope of the secant line through the two endpoints.
  • A rate of change at a single instant cannot be found with algebra alone, because the formula gives . Calculus finds it as the value that the average rates approach as the interval shrinks.
  • That limiting value is the instantaneous rate of change, the slope of the tangent line.
Average rate of change

Practice 1.1 · 2 questions

1.2

1.2 Defining Limits and Using Limit Notation

  • means that gets as close to as we like when is close enough to , with .
  • A limit describes behavior near . The value does not affect the limit and does not have to exist.
  • One-sided limits: approaches from the left and approaches from the right.
  • The two-sided limit exists only when both one-sided limits exist and are equal.
Two-sided limit

Practice 1.2 · 2 questions

1.3

1.3 Estimating Limit Values from Graphs

  • To read a limit from a graph, follow the curve toward from each side and find the -value it approaches. Ignore where the filled dot at is.
  • A limit does not exist when the two sides approach different values, when the function is unbounded near , or when the function oscillates without settling on one value.
  • A graph gives an estimate. Its scale can hide behavior close to .

Practice 1.3 · 2 questions

1.4

1.4 Estimating Limit Values from Tables

  • Choose inputs that approach from both sides and watch what the outputs approach.
  • If the outputs from both sides close in on the same number, that number is the estimated limit. If the two sides close in on different numbers, the limit does not exist.
  • A table suggests a limit but cannot prove it.

1.5

1.5 Determining Limits Using Algebraic Properties of Limits

  • When and both exist, the limit of a sum, difference, product, constant multiple, quotient, or power is found by applying that operation to the limits. For a quotient, the limit of the denominator must not be 0.
  • For a composition, when is continuous at that inner limit.
  • Direct substitution gives the limit whenever the function is continuous at .
Sum and difference
Product
Quotient

1.6

1.6 Determining Limits Using Algebraic Manipulation

  • When direct substitution gives , the limit may still exist. Rewrite the expression, cancel the common factor, then substitute.
  • Tools: factor and cancel, multiply by the conjugate to clear a square root, or combine the pieces of a complex fraction.
  • Cancelling is allowed because a limit uses only values of near , never itself.

  • Squeeze theorem: if for all near , and and have the same limit at , then .

1.9

1.9 Connecting Multiple Representations of Limits

  • A limit can be studied with a graph, a table, or algebra. All three must agree.
  • Graphs and tables give estimates. Algebra confirms the exact value.
  • The same fact looks different in each form: a common factor that cancels in the formula is a hole in the graph and a missing entry in the table whose neighbors approach one value.

Practice 1.9 · 1 question

1.10

1.10 Exploring Types of Discontinuities

  • Removable discontinuity: the limit exists, but is undefined or differs from the limit. The graph has a hole.
  • Jump discontinuity: both one-sided limits exist but they are not equal.
  • Infinite discontinuity: at least one one-sided limit is infinite. The graph has a vertical asymptote.

Practice 1.10 · 3 questions

1.11

1.11 Defining Continuity at a Point

  • A function is continuous at when three conditions hold: is defined, exists, and the limit equals .
  • To justify continuity on the exam, show that the left-hand limit, the right-hand limit, and the function value are all equal.
Continuity at a point

Practice 1.11 · 2 questions

1.12

1.12 Confirming Continuity over an Interval

  • A function is continuous on an interval when it is continuous at every point of the interval. At a closed endpoint, only the one-sided limit from inside the interval is used.
  • Polynomial, rational, power, exponential, logarithmic, and trigonometric functions are continuous at every point of their domains.
  • Sums, differences, products, quotients (where the denominator is not 0), and compositions of continuous functions are continuous.

Practice 1.12 · 2 questions

1.13

1.13 Removing Discontinuities

  • A removable discontinuity at is removed by defining or redefining to equal .
  • Jump and infinite discontinuities cannot be removed, because the two-sided limit does not exist.
  • For a piecewise function with an unknown constant, set the limit equal to the function value and solve.

Practice 1.13 · 2 questions

1.14

1.14 Connecting Infinite Limits and Vertical Asymptotes

  • If increases or decreases without bound as approaches from either side, we write the limit as or , and the line is a vertical asymptote.
  • For a rational function, look where the denominator is 0. A factor that cancels with the numerator gives a hole. A factor that does not cancel gives a vertical asymptote.
  • Find the sign of an infinite limit by checking the signs of the numerator and denominator just to the left or right of .

Watch outWriting a limit as describes how the function behaves. Strictly speaking, such a limit does not exist.

1.15

1.15 Connecting Limits at Infinity and Horizontal Asymptotes

  • If approaches as or as , the line is a horizontal asymptote. A graph can have two different horizontal asymptotes, and it can cross one.
  • For rational functions, compare degrees. Smaller degree on top: the limit is 0. Equal degrees: the limit is the ratio of the leading coefficients. Larger degree on top: there is no horizontal asymptote.
  • Growth rates as : logarithms grow more slowly than powers of , and powers of grow more slowly than exponential functions.
Growth rates

1.16

1.16 Working with the Intermediate Value Theorem (IVT)

  • Intermediate Value Theorem: if is continuous on and is any number between and , then there is at least one number in with .
  • The theorem guarantees that such a exists. It does not say where it is or how many there are.
  • State that is continuous on the closed interval before using the theorem. Without continuity, it gives no conclusion.
  • A sign change in a continuous function guarantees a zero between the two points.

2.1 Defining Average and Instantaneous Rates of Change at a Point

2.3 Estimating Derivatives of a Function at a Point

  • From a table, estimate with the average rate of change over the shortest interval that contains , preferably one with in the middle.
  • From a graph, estimate the slope of the tangent line at the point.
  • A derivative has units: the units of divided by the units of . Interpret it as a rate at one instant.

Practice 2.3 · 2 questions

2.4

2.4 Connecting Differentiability and Continuity: Determining When Derivatives Do and Do Not Exist

  • If is differentiable at , then is continuous at .
  • The converse is false. A function can be continuous at a point and still not be differentiable there.
  • A function is not differentiable where it has a discontinuity, a corner (the slopes from the left and right differ), a cusp, or a vertical tangent.
  • For a piecewise function to be differentiable where its pieces meet, the pieces must have the same value there and the same slope there.
